1.pericope_label: And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb. In the midst of the street of it, and on either side of the river, was there the tree of life, which bare twelve manner of fruits, and yielded her fruit every month: and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations. And there shall be no more curse: but the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it; and his servants shall serve him: And they shall see his face; and his name shall be in their foreheads. And there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light: and they shall reign for ever and ever.

schools.summary: Strike the adjective that the best manuscripts do not carry and read the river simply as water that is the emblem of life; line up the prophets who could not picture an age of blessing without a stream, and fix the allusion on the first Eden while marking the one difference that matters, that this water flows from the throne and not from the ground; then handle the tree as a question of number and of construction, whether the singular stands for a plural and whether the trees line the street or the riverbank, and settle the curse verse on the text, where the best copies read not curse but cursed person.

Take the river for the ever fresh and fruitful effluence of the Holy Ghost and send the reader to Ezekiel, where the trees also bear fruit every month; insist that the tree is not one but many, and that the leaves serve for the continuing of health rather than its restoring, since no sickness is there; then read the promised vision of the face as what was denied to Moses, the highest expression scripture has for the happiness of the heavenly state, and ask who the subjects of these reigning kings will be.

Read the numbers as figures of duration and doctrine, the twelve months intimating the whole time of life and the twelve fruits admitting the simpler sense that the cross bears fruit through the teaching of the twelve apostles; and distinguish fruit from leaves, so that if the fruit is the reward of a blessed immortality the leaves are rightly understood as a perpetual song, health to those who sing in their now blissful lot, where the true healing of the nations is full redemption and everlasting bliss.

Set the two descriptions side by side, since what was pictured before as a city is now pictured as a paradise — a paradise in a city, or a whole city in a paradise — and press the comparison with the garden that was lost, where two persons only tasted the pleasures of the place while here whole cities and nations find delight; then trace the river to its fountain-head at the throne of God and of the Lamb.

Clear the ground by refusal before building: the river is neither baptism, once administered in rivers and pools, nor the Holy Ghost, whose gifts are elsewhere likened to living water; and take the curse apart into its cause and its effects, sin on the one side and pain, sorrow and death on the other, finding none of them left in a state where the inhabitants are perfectly holy and their obedience complete.

debates.question: What is the river of the water of life?

sides.position: Neither baptism nor the Holy Ghost, since in this state there will be no use of ordinances
The ever fresh and fruitful effluence of the Holy Ghost
The emblem of life in its gladness, purity, activity and fulness, after the manner of the prophets who pictured blessing as a stream
Eden's river recovered, save that it flows from the throne and not out of the ground

debates.question: Where does the tree of life stand, and is it one tree or many?

sides.position: Trees rather than one, the singular standing for the plural since it is both in the streets and on each side of the river
Between the street and the river, the whole stream lined on either side with two rows of it
In the streets as well as on the banks, abounding everywhere, which gives the more beautiful image

outliers.note: Alone presses the paradox of the two figures against each other — a paradise in a city, or a whole city in a paradise — and contrasts the two persons who tasted the first garden with the whole nations who will delight in this one.

Alone asks who the subjects of the reigning saints will be, and answers that they are the other inhabitants of the new earth, since a difference must remain between those who excelled in virtue and those saved as by fire.

themes: the river of water of life

6.pericope_label: And he said unto me, These sayings are faithful and true: and the Lord God of the holy prophets sent his angel to shew unto his servants the things which must shortly be done. Behold, I come quickly: blessed is he that keepeth the sayings of the prophecy of this book. And I John saw these things, and heard them. And when I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel which shewed me these things. Then saith he unto me, See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets, and of them which keep the sayings of this book: worship God.

schools.summary: Mark the seam where the epilogue begins and say what has been finished, the enemies quelled and the affairs of the world wound up, so that only a few closing matters remain; take the attestation to cover the whole book rather than the last vision only, resting the point on language that echoes the opening verse; reckon the promised speed on God's scale rather than ours; and treat the prostration as natural though wrong, the more understandable because Christ's own voice had followed the angel's.

Divide the remainder of the book into its three movements, the angel affirming what has been spoken, Christ confirming it and pledging himself for the fulfilment, and the seer warning against adding or diminishing before the closing blessing; state without softening the difficulty that many sayings taken literally would mean fulfilment soon after delivery; and notice that the words of the reproof here are identical with an earlier scene, so that the question arises whether this is the same incident related again rather than the apostle repeating a fault of which he had been solemnly warned.

Make the ratification solemn and wide, confirmed by the name and nature of the God who gave the discoveries, by the messengers chosen, since God would not employ his saints and angels to deceive the world, and by the accomplishment soon to follow; and note that some extend the words beyond this vision and beyond this book to the completing and confirming of the canon itself.

Refuse to let the promise of quick coming be spent on a past event, since the coming in power against Jerusalem was over before this book was written, so that the second and personal coming to judgment must be meant; and keep the speakers straight throughout, the angel talking with the seer in one verse and Christ himself in the next, while the seer's own name is set down to make what he witnessed the more surely believed.

debates.question: What do the faithful and true sayings cover?

sides.position: The whole book, not merely the preceding vision, as the language echoing the opening verse proves
This book and this last vision, though some extend it to the whole New Testament and to the completing of the canon
The whole book, whose conclusion agrees exactly with its introduction

debates.question: Is the prostration before the angel the same incident as the earlier one?

sides.position: Very probably the same incident related again, since the words and the reproof are identical and the apostle had been solemnly warned already
A second and natural though wrong act, the more understandable because Christ's own voice had followed the angel's
A second act, John being overcome by the revelation and perhaps suspecting that the Redeemer himself was manifesting himself

outliers.note: Alone proposes that the prostration before the angel is not a second fault but the same incident related again, on the ground that the words and the reproof are identical with the earlier scene.

Alone states without softening that many sayings in the book, taken literally, would mean the prophecies were to be fulfilled soon after their delivery, and notes that this is a strong support for one whole scheme of interpretation.

10.pericope_label: And he saith unto me, Seal not the sayings of the prophecy of this book: for the time is at hand. He that is unjust, let him be unjust still: and he which is filthy, let him be filthy still: and he that is righteous, let him be righteous still: and he that is holy, let him be holy still. And, behold, I come quickly; and my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last. Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city. For without are dogs, and sorcerers, and whoremongers, and murderers, and idolaters, and whosoever loveth and maketh a lie.

schools.summary: Set the command not to seal against the older prophets, who were told to seal because their prophecies related to far-distant times and the record was to be laid up for future ages; sharpen the contrast into a difference of dispensations, the one preliminary and the other final, since however long the gospel age lasts it is the last time; call the licence given to the unjust probably ironical and in no sense a commendation, a picture of the hopelessness of the final state; and note that the first of the divine titles is applied to God twice in this book and here alone to Christ, the crowning proof of his deity.

Read the refusal to seal as a matter of nearness rather than of dispensation, since the sayings are not to be laid up for future generations but concern the present, and what concerned the Jews was certainly at hand; take the licence to the unjust as urgency, that fulfilment will come so suddenly there is little space for repentance and what is done must be done instantly; and press the Greek behind the word right, rendering it authority over the tree of life, founded on obedience and that obedience produced by grace.

Rule out the readings that will not stand before offering one, since the licence given to the unjust is neither irony, nor a permission, nor a threat dressed as a licence; take the sealing clause as Christ's own words and record that a version omits it; and read the last beatitude of the book in the received form, where the commandments done evangelically, in the strength of Christ and without dependence on them, are what the blessing rests upon.

debates.question: Why is this prophecy not to be sealed, when Daniel's was?

sides.position: Because the dispensations differ: the one preliminary and prefatory, the other completive and final, so that the gospel age is the last time
Because the sayings concern the present rather than future generations, and what concerned the Jews was at hand
Because the older prophecies related to far-distant times and were to be laid up, while this book is to be left open for all to read

debates.question: What does it mean to let the unjust be unjust still?

sides.position: Neither irony, nor a permission, nor a threat dressed as a licence, but a prophecy
A declaration about the state beyond the judgment, where all is fixed and unchanging
Probably ironical, a picture of the hopelessness of the final state and no commendation of it
A warning of urgency, since fulfilment will come so suddenly that little space is left for repentance

debates.question: Does the last beatitude bless those who do the commandments or those who wash their robes?

sides.position: Those that wash their robes, the reading of two of the best manuscripts, which points to a refuge from the power of sin
Those that do his commandments, done evangelically in the strength of Christ and without dependence on them

outliers.note: Alone reports that a modern editor rejects the verse about the unjust as unlike John, and answers it by reading the language as ironical rather than as a commendation of the lost estate.

Alone renders the word for right as authority over the tree of life, and builds a chain from it: without grace no obedience, without obedience no authority, without authority no right, without right no enjoyment.

16.pericope_label: I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star. And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.

schools.summary: Call the naming of Jesus the last and most solemn attestation in the book, and insist it is the Jesus of history speaking who is also the Christ of theology; read the address to the churches as reaching the seven directly and all churches remotely; explain the first title botanically rather than genealogically, as the root-shoot that starts up from a fallen stock rather than the stock from which a tree grows; and hold both directions of the closing invitation together, since the book ends with the cry that the coming One would come while those who thirst for his coming are bidden to come to him.

Identify the callers historically as the prophets and the apostles, the church under the old covenant and the church under the new, inviting men to Jesus that they may be saved; keep the astronomy of the second title working, since as the morning star ushers in the sun so he ushers in the unclouded and eternal glories, and reach back for the star out of Jacob; and press the last clause to its limit, that no soul is excluded and whoever wills may take the water of life without money or price.

Set the signature beside the seer's own, so that as John gave his name to what he witnessed Christ puts his to what he authored, which is at once a claim on the reader's attention and a declaration of who it is that speaks of his coming; and locate the closing cry inside the believer, the Spirit of God in the hearts of his people filling them with love of that appearing, so that he may be said to wish for it in them as he is said elsewhere to cry Abba in them.

debates.question: How can Christ be both the root and the offspring of David?

sides.position: Root not in the sense that David sprang from him, but as the root-shoot that starts up from a fallen stock
Root as to his divine nature, since from him the whole race sprang, and offspring as to his human, taken of the stock of David
David's Lord and David's Son at once, possessing David's throne

debates.question: Whom does the closing Come address?

sides.position: The Lord Jesus: the Spirit and the bride answer the voice just heard and plead for his coming
Men: the construction demands it, the verse being a summary of all the invitations of mercy
Both, since the book ends with the cry that the coming One would come, yet those who thirst are bidden to come to him

outliers.note: Alone adds the historical observation that the whole regal family of David terminated in Christ, so that as he lives for ever he is the only true and everlasting David.

Alone argues the construction of the closing invitation the other way from the rest, holding that the Spirit and the bride address men rather than Christ, and that nothing could be more fitting at the close of the volume than an announcement that salvation is free to all.

themes: the root and offspring of David

18.pericope_label: For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book: And if any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life, and out of the holy city, and from the things which are written in this book. He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

schools.summary: Leave the speaker of the closing warning genuinely open and name the parties to the dispute — one who rejects the verses as an interpolation out of harmony with the book, one who takes them for the seer's own warning drawn from Deuteronomy, one who holds them to come from Jesus himself; suggest what corruption John may have foreseen, that when the passages describing Antichrist came to be fulfilled those to whom they applied would strike them out; and note that grace is an unusual close for an apocalypse though suitable for a book meant to be read in the churches.

Widen adding and taking away from copying to construing, so that adding is giving any other meaning or application than God intends and taking away is curtailing the sense or explaining away the spirit and design; then apply the warning to oneself with unusual candour, confessing that it has prevented the indulging of one's own conjectures or the adopting of another's, the subject being too awful to trifle with where the meaning is obscure, and leaving such things to time and event as the surest interpreters; and treat the sanction as guarding the whole New Testament, as Moses guarded the law.

Hear the last exchange as a leave-taking, in which Christ, having shown these things to his people on earth, seems to part from them and return to heaven, yet parts in great kindness and with the promise of a speedy return, just as at the ascension he parted with a promise of his presence; and answer the objection that so many ages have passed since the words were written with the reminder that he is not slack to his people.

Settle the speaker from the shape of the passage rather than from conjecture, since the book is not yet finished and both Christ and the seer speak after this, so the words can be neither a copyist's adjuration nor the writer's own; and draw the line of subtraction at practices rather than manuscripts, counting as taking away the denying of the book's authority, the withholding of it from the people, and the wilful perverting of its sense so that what it says of antichrist shall not be found to apply.

debates.question: Who speaks the warning against adding and taking away?

sides.position: The writer himself, guarding his book against interpolation
Christ, since the book is not yet finished and both Christ and John speak after this
Jesus himself, still bearing solemn witness to the book
Nobody in the book: the verses are an interpolation, out of harmony with the rest

outliers.note: Alone turns the warning on himself, confessing that it has weighed on his mind and kept him from indulging his own conjectures about the book or adopting those of others, and leaving such things to time and event as the surest interpreters.
Alone infers from the warning that books were already liable to corruption by addition or omission in the apostle’s own day, or at least were felt to be.
